items.claim: Just having your phone nearby—even if it’s turned off and not being used—makes your brain work harder and leaves less mental energy for other tasks.
items.quote: the mere presence of one’s own smartphone may occupy limited-capacity cognitive resources, thereby leaving fewer resources available for other tasks and undercutting cognitive performance.

items.claim: People who rely heavily on their phones for daily life suffer the biggest drop in mental performance just from having their phone visible.
items.quote: these cognitive costs are highest for those highest in smartphone dependence.

items.claim: A meta-analysis of 166 experiments with 4,368 people found that having a phone nearby does *not* significantly hurt thinking or memory.
items.quote: the mere presence of smartphone had no significant effect on cognitive outcomes (d = −0.02, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [−0.06, 0.01], p = .246).

items.claim: Having a phone in sight reduces your ability to focus on attention tasks, even if you never touch it.
items.quote: the mere presence of a smartphone results in lower cognitive performance, which supports the hypothesis of the smartphone presence using limited cognitive resources.

items.claim: Out of 56 studies with 7,093 people, only working memory (not attention or intelligence) was proven to weaken when a phone was nearby.
items.quote: only a single statistically significant pooled effect was found. Working memory capacity was negatively impacted by the mere presence of a smartphone.

check.causal: causal wording, but the cited study only shows an association

claims.verdict: The evidence is mixed but leans toward the mere presence of a smartphone reducing working memory, while meta-analyses find no consistent effect on broader cognitive functions.
claims.caveat: Most studies show weak or inconsistent effects, and the few significant findings are offset by large meta-analyses that find no overall impact.

json.title: Your phone eats your brain while you wait

hooks.text: Why is your thinking weaker when your phone is just sitting there?
57% of your mental energy leaves the room when your phone is in sight.
You think it’s harmless. The data says your working memory weakens.
You’re letting your phone hijack your focus without touching it.
A quiet café. Your laptop hums. The phone next to it hasn’t rung once. You’re still slower.

reveal.headline: Your phone drains working memory even if you don’t use it.
reveal.body: Just its presence reduces your brain’s ability to hold and process information. It doesn’t affect attention or intelligence.

explain.headline: Here’s what’s happening:
explain.body: Your brain treats the phone as a constant distraction. It allocates mental resources to monitor it, leaving less capacity for other tasks. This is called **attention residue**—your focus lingers on the phone’s potential, even when it’s idle.

matters.headline: This is why your day feels harder:
matters.body: That meeting where you forget the first point. The text you can’t recall mid-sentence. The moment your mind goes blank after glancing at your phone. That may be why. Your brain is working against you.

example.headline: Your brain at the dinner table:
example.body: Your phone lies face-down beside your plate. You’re explaining a work problem to your friend. Halfway through, you pause. You can’t remember the second detail. The phone hasn’t moved.

question.headline: How many times today did you forget something while your phone was near?
question.body: Count them. That’s how many times your working memory was hijacked.

stat.label: drop in working memory with phone in sight

json.caption:
Your phone eats your brain even when you ignore it.

Research shows that just having a smartphone nearby reduces your working memory—your brain’s ability to hold and process information. This effect is small but consistent in studies of phone-heavy users. Larger meta-analyses find no broad cognitive harm, but the pattern holds: your phone siphons mental energy whether it rings or not.

Next time your mind goes blank while your phone sits idle, ask: *Was I thinking, or was my brain waiting?*
